context.motion: Does the Kalam cosmological argument show that the universe began to exist, has a cause, and points to a personal creator?

routes.description: The defender’s route applies the causal principle to a universe whose finite temporal beginning is established by arguments against an actual infinite and against formation by successive addition, then identifies a personal agent as the best explanation of the universe’s first effect.
routes.successCriteria: Establish that the past is finite, that the universe consequently began and has a cause, and that an eternal impersonal mechanism cannot explain a temporally first universe whereas personal agency can.

bridges.description: The Kalam shows that the universe began to exist, has a cause, and points to a personal creator.
A beginningless past would contain an actually infinite number of events; because such an actual infinite cannot exist, the temporal series and universe began.
Hilbert-style concrete scenarios reveal that an actually infinite collection is metaphysically impossible, despite the consistency of infinite set theory.
An actually infinite temporal series cannot be formed by successive addition or completed by counting down from a beginningless past.
An eternal impersonal cause would produce its effect eternally or not at all, while a personal agent can freely originate a temporally first universe.

routes.description: The critic’s route argues that the Kalam does not exclude a beginningless material reality and that its paradoxes and conceptual analysis leave coherent infinite-past and impersonal-cause alternatives available.
routes.successCriteria: Show that actual-infinite scenarios establish strangeness rather than impossibility, that successive-addition reasoning does not rule out a beginningless series ending in the present, or that an impersonal indeterministic cause can explain a first universe without a personal creator.

bridges.description: The Kalam does not show that the universe began to exist, has a cause, and points to a personal creator.
The Kalam’s finitude and personhood inferences fail to exclude coherent beginningless-past or impersonal-origin alternatives, so its conclusion is not established.
The unusual behavior of Hilbert’s Hotel does not entail that an actually infinite collection is metaphysically impossible.
The impossibility of reaching the end of an endless count does not establish the impossibility of reaching the present end of a beginningless countdown.
An impersonal indeterministic cause could originate the universe at one time, so a personal cause is not uniquely required.
